title: Gastroesophageal Junction and Pylorus Distensibility Before and After Sleeve Gastrectomy—pilot Study with EndoFlipTM
question: Does sleeve gastrectomy change how easily the gastroesophageal junction and the pylorus open when a balloon is filled inside them, and is that linked to reflux a year later?

bottom_line.question: Does sleeve gastrectomy change how easily the gastroesophageal junction and the pylorus open when a balloon is filled inside them, and is that linked to reflux a year later?
bottom_line.answer: In this nine-patient pilot, the distensibility index of the gastroesophageal junction at 40 ml was higher a year after sleeve gastrectomy than before (1.4 vs 2.9 mm2/mmHg, p value=0.046), and the pylorus index rose as well. The authors say larger studies are needed.

provenance.quote: EndoFlipTM at 40 ml the DI of the GEJ was significantly higher post-SG compared to the presurgical assessment (1.4 mm2/mmHg [1.1-2.6] vs. 2.9 mm2/mmHg [2.6–5.3], p value=0.046)

sections.title: Why Reflux After Sleeve Gastrectomy Matters
sections.markdown: Sleeve gastrectomy is a weight-loss operation that removes most of the stomach and leaves a narrow tube. Its main drawback is acid reflux, known as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Some patients develop reflux for the first time after the operation, and others find that reflux they already had gets worse. Reflux lowers quality of life and raises the risk of long-term complications. The **gastroesophageal junction** (GEJ) plays a large part in it. This is the valve where the oesophagus meets the stomach, and it normally keeps acid down. The pylorus, the valve at the stomach's exit, may also matter.

sections.title: Measuring How Easily the Valves Stretch
sections.markdown:
The team used EndoFlip, a balloon probe passed down through the mouth that measures how easily a valve stretches open. Its reading is the distensibility index (DI), measured in square millimetres per mmHg:

DI = cross-sectional area of the opening / pressure in the balloon

A higher DI means a looser valve. The authors expected surgery to loosen both the GEJ and the pylorus.

sections.title: Patients and Study Design
sections.markdown: Nine adults with a BMI of 35 or more were treated at a Swiss university hospital in 2018. Each was measured before surgery, during it and one year later, with the balloon filled to 40 ml. They also had endoscopy, oesophageal pressure testing and pH-impedance monitoring. GERD was defined as acid in the lower oesophagus more than 6% of the time plus more than 80 reflux episodes.

sections.title: Key Results
sections.markdown:
Main findings:

- The GEJ loosened after surgery. Its median DI rose from 1.4 to 2.9 (p = 0.046).
- The pylorus loosened too, from 6.0 to 13.1 (p = 0.046). This may be linked to faster stomach emptying. An earlier study by Desprez and colleagues did not find this change.
- Seven patients had complete reflux data. The four who had reflux at one year (new or continuing) already had looser GEJs before surgery than the three who did not (median DI 2.6 vs 0.5, p = 0.031). Measurements taken during and after surgery did not separate the two groups.
- Weight loss was similar in both groups.

sections.title: What It Means and What Comes Next
sections.markdown: Earlier studies measured these valves only in the operating room. This is the first to follow them with EndoFlip for a full year after sleeve gastrectomy. The results suggest that a loose GEJ before surgery may predict reflux afterward. Nine patients are too few to confirm this, and EndoFlip still lacks normal reference values, so larger studies are needed.

sources.Sec1/p1: A major drawback of sleeve gastrectomy (SG) is the postoperative development of “de novo” or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) [–]. GERD is considered a risk factor for long-term complications and decreases the quality of life [–]. The gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) (often also referred to as the lower esophageal sphincter) plays an essential role in the complex pathophysiology of GERD, and a better understanding of the associated anatomical and functions is necessary. To date, the usefulness of an endoscopic functional luminal imaging probe (EndoFlip™) in bariatric patients before and after SG to assess the pathophysiological changes in the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and pylorus with regard to GERD is poorly described. We hypothesized that SG leads to increased distensibility indices (DI) of the GEJ and the pylorus.
sources.Sec2/p1: This prospective diagnostic observational study included patients (informed consent, ≥18 years, BMI ≥35 kg/m2, fulfillment of the Swiss Society for the Study of morbid obesity and metabolic disorders guidelines criteria) undergoing elective SG at a tertiary care university hospital. The study was approved by the local ethics committee (BASEC ID 2017-00923). Exclusion criteria were pregnancy or breastfeeding, oral anticoagulant, known bleeding disorder, and contraindication for endoscopic examination. Patients underwent esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD), pH-impedance monitoring, high-resolution manometry, and EndoFlip™ (Crospon Medical Devices, Galway, Ireland). GERD was defined (Lyon Consensus 2018) as distal oesophageal acid (pH<4) exposure time >6% and a total number of reflux episodes >80 (as per pH-impedance monitoring) [] and was differentiated between no, stable, de novo, or resolved status when comparing pre and postoperative data. Bariatric outcomes were reported in accordance with the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) guidelines []. Statistical analysis (categorical by Pearson chi-square test and continuous by Mann–Whitney U test) was performed using SPSS Statistics version 25 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York).
